title: The Toy Train Wreck to the Twenty-Second EGOT: Spielberg, the Suburb, and the Archive of Testimony
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Backyard and the Eight-Millimeter Camera

stops.name: Cincinnati, born to an engineer and a pianist
stops.date_confidence: attested for the birth. The grandmother's English lessons and the tattooed-forearm memory are undated in the sources and are placed at the earliest household the record gives him; the city is inferred from the family's residence, not stated.
stops.campa: A son is born in a Cincinnati hospital to Arnold Spielberg, an electrical engineer who will help build early computers, and Leah Posner, a concert pianist. The household keeps Orthodox observance, and close by it is his grandmother's table, where she teaches English to Hungarian survivors of the camps. In the break, while the others eat and nobody is learning anything, one of the men rolls back his sleeve and points at the numbers tattooed there. That is a two, he says. That is a four.
stops.quote: One man in particular, I kept looking at his numbers, his number tattooed on his forearm... he started, you know, when, during the dinner break, when everybody was eating and not learning, he would point to the numbers. And he would say, that is a two, and that is a four...
stops.quote_source: Steven Spielberg, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Steven Spielberg', article note 19, recalling a Holocaust survivor his grandmother taught
suggested_refs: Joseph McBride, Steven Spielberg: A Biography (1997), on the Cincinnati household and Arnold Spielberg's engineering career
sources: Joseph McBride, Steven Spielberg: A Biography (1997)
Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences biographical record

stops.name: Haddon Township, the move east for RCA
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1952 in Wikipedia; month and day defaulted. One reachable dossier item gave the range as c. 1949-1953, which contradicts the same dossier's own chronology and is not followed here. The family leaves for Phoenix in early 1957.
stops.campa: Arnold Spielberg takes a job with RCA and the family moves east to a township across the Delaware from Philadelphia. Steven is five. The street outside is new and flat and filling with the children of other engineers; inside, the household keeps kosher and keeps Hebrew, and the boy is aware of the difference between the two. Five years pass here, in the ordinary postwar American suburb whose cul-de-sacs and picture windows he will spend a career photographing. Then his father is hired somewhere else, and the family goes west.
suggested_refs: Joseph McBride, Steven Spielberg: A Biography (1997), on the New Jersey years
sources: Joseph McBride, Steven Spielberg: A Biography (1997)

stops.name: Arcadia, Phoenix, the train wreck filmed once
stops.date_confidence: attested to early 1957 for the move; month and day defaulted. The Arizona years run to the Saratoga move of 1964. The Eagle Scout award and the bar mitzvah are attested but not separately dated in the pool.
stops.campa: The family settles in the Arcadia district under Camelback Mountain. His father owns an eight-millimeter camera and a Lionel train set, and the boy crashes the trains again and again to watch the collision from floor level. Then it occurs to him to film the wreck once and run the film as often as he likes. He recruits neighborhood children as crews and casualties, stages battles in the yard, and charges admission at the door. In the same Arizona years he earns his Eagle Scout badge and prepares for his bar mitzvah.
stops.quote: The trains went around and around, and after a while that got boring, and I had this eight-millimeter camera, and I staged a train wreck and filmed it.
stops.quote_source: Steven Spielberg, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Steven Spielberg', article note 35
suggested_refs: DGA Quarterly, 'Age & Innocence' interview (2006), on the backyard 8mm films

stops.name: Arcadia High School, Escape to Nowhere
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged, not resolved: Wikipedia puts the film at age thirteen, c. 1959-60, and the dossier chronology says 1959; one geography item said 1961. Month and day defaulted. The school coordinate here is 4703 E Indian School Rd; a coordinate circulating in the pool sat about three kilometres northwest of campus.
stops.campa: At around thirteen he makes a forty-minute war picture called Escape to Nowhere, casting schoolmates as soldiers and shooting on his father's camera. It takes a statewide amateur prize. The film is a war film because his father's war is the household's constant subject, told at the table by men who had been in it, and because a camera pointed at a boy falling into Arizona dirt can be made to mean North Africa. The year is given as 1959, and also as 1961, and nobody has settled it.
stops.quote: my dad told me stories about World War II constantly... I knew, based on the stories my dad and his friends were telling about World War II, that there was no glory in war.
stops.quote_source: Steven Spielberg, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Steven Spielberg', article note 19
suggested_refs: John Baxter, Steven Spielberg: The Unauthorised Biography (1996), on the Phoenix amateur productions
sources: John Baxter, Steven Spielberg: The Unauthorised Biography (1996)

stops.name: Phoenix Little Theatre, Firelight for one night
stops.date_confidence: attested: premiere 24 March 1964 at the Phoenix Little Theatre, budget 500 dollars, gross 501 dollars, per the Wikipedia article on the film. The coordinate is the theatre's North Central Avenue site and is approximate; no primary source in the pool gives the venue's location.
stops.campa: At seventeen he finishes Firelight, a science-fiction feature about lights in the sky, financed by his father with five hundred dollars. He rents the Phoenix Little Theatre for one evening, sells tickets at the door, and takes five hundred and one dollars: a profit of one dollar. Thirteen years later he will make the same picture again with a studio behind him and call it Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Of Firelight itself, only about three minutes and forty seconds have ever been shown in public.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'Firelight (1964 film)', for the premiere date, budget, gross and surviving footage

stops.name: Saratoga, the last year of school
stops.date_confidence: attested for graduation from Saratoga High School in 1965; month and day defaulted. The family move is dated after the March 1964 Firelight premiere. The coordinate is 20300 Herriman Ave; a coordinate circulating in the pool sat about 900 metres off.
stops.campa: The family moves north to Saratoga after the Firelight premiere, for his last year of school, and the year is the worst of his life. He is the Jewish boy in a school with almost none, and the school makes him pay for it: smacked, kicked, two bloody noses, by his own later account. He graduates in 1965 with grades no film school will look at. His parents' marriage is coming apart in the same house in the same season. Nothing reachable dates the divorce itself.
stops.quote: In high school, I got smacked and kicked around. Two bloody noses. It was horrible.
stops.quote_source: Steven Spielberg, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Steven Spielberg', article note 30, on antisemitic bullying in high school
suggested_refs: Saratoga High School alumni records, cited via DGA Quarterly (2006)

stops.name: University of Southern California, the rejection
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1965 in the Jewish Virtual Library entry and in McBride; month and day defaulted. The number of applications is not fixed by any source reached here.
stops.campa: He applies to the film school at the University of Southern California, whose graduates already run a good part of the industry he means to enter, and is turned down for mediocre grades. How many times he applied is not fixed by any source. He never studies film formally, then or later. Three decades on the same university will hold the largest archive of Holocaust survivor testimony in the world, because he builds it and hands it to them, and he will come onto this campus as a donor.
suggested_refs: USC School of Cinematic Arts admissions history; USC Shoah Foundation institutional history, sfi.usc.edu
sources: Joseph McBride, Steven Spielberg: A Biography (1997)

stops.name: Universal Studios, the unofficial apprentice
stops.date_confidence: tradition, not record. Wikipedia's sourced version has a chance conversation with an executive during a tour producing a three-day pass, a fourth day walked in without one, and roughly two months as an unofficial apprentice that summer. The restroom stall and the two and a half months five days a week are retelling. Month set to open the summer.
stops.campa: He gets onto the Universal lot the first time on a tour, falls into conversation with an executive, and comes away with a three-day pass. On the fourth day he walks up to the gate without one and the guard waves him through. He spends roughly two months of that summer inside, watching soundstages work and asking questions nobody stops him from asking. He will tell the story for the rest of his life, and the tellings change: the pass drops out of it, a restroom stall enters it. Which version he himself believes is not recoverable.
stops.quote: I basically spent the next two months at Universal Studios... that was how I became an unofficial apprentice that summer.
stops.quote_source: Steven Spielberg, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Steven Spielberg', article note 56
suggested_refs: The New Yorker, 'Steven Spielberg at Seventy' (2017), for his own later retellings of the lot story
sources: The New Yorker, 'Steven Spielberg at Seventy' (2017)

stops.name: California State University, Long Beach, enrolled in English
stops.date_confidence: attested for enrolment in 1965 and completion of the degree in 2002; the September start month is conventional for the academic year and is not separately sourced.
stops.campa: He enrolls at California State University, Long Beach, and reads English, because English is what they will let him read. He is a poor student for the second time in three years, and he leaves without a degree the moment Universal offers him paid work. In 2002, fifty-five years old and holding two Academy Awards for directing, he finishes the coursework by independent study and takes the bachelor's degree at last. One of the credits is granted for Schindler's List, submitted as coursework.
suggested_refs: California State University, Long Beach commencement records for 2002
sources: California State University, Long Beach commencement records, cited via news coverage of the 2002 degree

stops.name: Universal City, Amblin' and Sidney Sheinberg
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1968 for the short and the contract; month and day defaulted. His exact age at signing is given variously as twenty-one and twenty-two across the sources reached.
stops.campa: He shoots Amblin', twenty-six minutes on thirty-five millimetre, two hitchhikers crossing the desert toward the Pacific, no dialogue at all. Sidney Sheinberg, a Universal vice president, sees it and offers a seven-year contract to direct television, making him the youngest director signed to a long-term deal by a major American studio. He signs, and he drops out of Long Beach State. He is twenty-one at the signing, or twenty-two; the sources disagree and the disagreement is not resolved.
suggested_refs: Amblin', 26 min, 35mm (1968); Amblin official corporate biography, amblin.com

stops.name: Universal City, Night Gallery and the contract years
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1969 for the Night Gallery debut and to 1971 for the series episodes named; months and days defaulted, and the two years are collapsed into one stop at the studio that assigned all of them.
stops.campa: His professional debut is the Eyes episode of Night Gallery, written by Rod Serling, starring Joan Crawford at the far end of her career and directed by a man of twenty-two. She plays a blind woman who buys twelve hours of sight. Then come the assignments a contract director gets: Marcus Welby M.D., The Name of the Game, Owen Marshall Counselor at Law, The Psychiatrist, and Murder by the Book, the first Columbo after the pilots, in which a man in a raincoat wears a murderer down by refusing to leave the room.
suggested_refs: Night Gallery, 'Eyes' (1969); Columbo, 'Murder by the Book' (1971)

stops.name: Soledad Canyon, the truck with no driver
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1971 for Duel; month and day defaulted. The filming corridor north of Los Angeles is production-history consensus and is not confirmed to landmark precision by any source reached here.
stops.campa: Universal gives him a television movie: a salesman on a two-lane desert road, a tanker truck behind him, and no explanation offered for why the truck wants him dead. The driver is never seen, only boots and a forearm out of a window. He shoots it in the dry canyons north of Los Angeles and gets a picture that runs entirely on withheld information. It is promoted out of television into theatres, and it is the discovery he will make again three years later on the water off Massachusetts.
suggested_refs: Duel (1971), Universal television film, later given theatrical release in Europe

stops.name: Universal City, The Sugarland Express
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1974 for the release and the Cannes screenplay prize; month and day defaulted. Spielberg's own presence at Cannes is not documented in the pool, so the stop is placed at the studio that made the film.
stops.campa: His first theatrical feature follows a Texas woman who breaks her husband out of a prison farm to recover their child from foster care, and the long line of patrol cars that follows the pair across the state without firing. It takes the screenplay prize at Cannes, though nothing in the record places Spielberg himself in the room. Almost no audience turns up for it, and Universal takes the loss. John Williams writes the score, the first of a collaboration that will run five decades.
suggested_refs: The Sugarland Express (1974); Cannes Film Festival prize records for 1974

stops.name: Menemsha, Martha's Vineyard, the shark that would not work
stops.date_confidence: attested: principal photography 2 May to 6 October 1974, 159 days against a planned 55, per the Wikipedia article on the film. The picture releases in 1975; the coordinate is Menemsha, the confirmed primary Vineyard location.
stops.campa: Universal sends him to Martha's Vineyard to shoot a novel about a shark, and the Atlantic ruins him. The mechanical animal sinks, corrodes, and will not work in salt water; a fifty-five day schedule runs to a hundred and fifty-nine, from the second of May to the sixth of October; he is certain, out on the boat, that he will never be hired again. Unable to show the shark, he shoots its absence: a yellow barrel moving against the tide, two notes in the orchestra, the camera set at the level of a swimmer's eye. The film opens the following summer.
suggested_refs: Carl Gottlieb, The Jaws Log (1975), the daily record of the Vineyard shoot

stops.name: Devils Tower, the summons in the sky
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1977; month and day defaulted. Correction carried: Close Encounters won one competitive Academy Award, for cinematography; the sound-effects-editing honour to Frank Warner was a Special Achievement Award, not a competitive category.
stops.campa: He writes this one as well as directs it, and what he writes is Firelight again: lights over a suburban road, a man taken over by a shape he cannot explain, a government that knows more than it says. The climax is staged at the real Devils Tower, a stone column standing alone out of the Wyoming grassland. The French director Francois Truffaut plays the scientist who reads the sky. The ending has an ordinary father walk away from his wife and children and onto a spaceship, and the film's photography takes an Academy Award.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'Close Encounters of the Third Kind', for the awards record and the Devils Tower staging
sources: Wikipedia, 'Close Encounters of the Third Kind'

segments.name: Amblin: the Suburb and the Serial

stops.name: Universal City, Amblin Entertainment and the Ark
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged: Wikipedia dates Amblin Entertainment's founding to 1975, with Kathleen Kennedy and Frank Marshall joining in 1980, while the widely cited 1981 date belongs to the Kennedy and Marshall company. The date here is that arrival year, not a first founding. 1941 released 1979; Raiders released 1981.
stops.campa: After 1941, a war comedy that costs a fortune, earns ninety-two million dollars and is savaged everywhere, he stops working alone. Kathleen Kennedy and Frank Marshall come aboard the production company he calls Amblin, after the short that got him through the Universal gate, and it works out of a bungalow on the backlot. George Lucas hands him a serial: a man in a hat, a bullwhip, a Nazi expedition after the Ark of the Covenant. Raiders of the Lost Ark sweeps the craft categories at the Academy Awards.
suggested_refs: Amblin official corporate biography, amblin.com; Bungalow 477 on the Universal backlot

stops.name: Northridge, the creature in the closet
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1982; month and day defaulted. Gross figures corrected: 797.3 million dollars cumulative across all releases, roughly 619 million on the 1982-83 original run. Four competitive Academy Awards: score, sound, sound effects editing, visual effects.
stops.campa: He shoots a film about a boy whose father has left, in tract houses in the San Fernando Valley, with the camera held at the height of a ten-year-old so that adults come into frame from the waist down. The creature in the closet is the friend the divorce owes him. E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial takes four Academy Awards: score, sound, sound effects editing, visual effects. Across all its releases it earns close to eight hundred million dollars, of which some six hundred and nineteen million come from the original run of 1982 and 1983.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial', for the awards and the release-by-release grosses
sources: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences filmography records

stops.name: Simi Valley, the house over the cemetery
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1982; the day given is the film's release. The Directors Guild inquiry and the 15,000 dollar arbitration award to Hooper are attested; the extent of Spielberg's direction on set is disputed by the participants and is not resolved here.
stops.campa: The same year, barred by a contract clause from directing two pictures at once, he writes a story about a tract house built on a cemetery and hands the direction to Tobe Hooper. Crew accounts put Spielberg on the set constantly, storyboarding, choosing shots. The Directors Guild opens an inquiry; an arbitrator orders the studio to pay Hooper fifteen thousand dollars; Spielberg publishes a letter affirming that Hooper directed the film. Dominique Dunne is murdered that year, and Heather O'Rourke dies at twelve of a misdiagnosis, and people begin to say the picture is cursed. Who directed it is still disputed by the people who were there.
suggested_refs: Los Angeles Times contemporaneous reporting on the Poltergeist credit dispute; reverseshot.org, 'Poltergeist: Two Takes'
sources: Los Angeles Times reporting on the credit dispute, cited in reverseshot.org

stops.name: Kandy, Sri Lanka standing in for India
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1984 for release and for meeting Kate Capshaw on set; month and day defaulted. The relocation of the India-set sequences is production-history consensus; India's exact objections are not documented to primary-source level in the pool.
stops.campa: India reads the script and will not have it shot there, so the India of Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom is Sri Lanka, hill country near Kandy standing in for a palace where the British are served chilled monkey brains and children are worked underground by a cult that tears out hearts. The film is dark enough that the American ratings board invents PG-13 to hold it. On the set he meets Kate Capshaw, who is playing the nightclub singer. He marries her seven years later.
stops.quote: It was a good learning exercise for me to really throw myself into a black hole. I came out of the darkness of Temple Of Doom and I entered the light of the woman I was eventually going to marry and raise a family with.
stops.quote_source: Steven Spielberg, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Steven Spielberg', article note 120
suggested_refs: The PG-13 rating, introduced by the Motion Picture Association in 1984

stops.name: Los Angeles, the birth of Max and the napkin
stops.date_confidence: attested: Max Samuel born 13 June 1985, marriage to Amy Irving November 1985, divorce 1989, settlement reported near 100 million dollars after a judge vacated a prenuptial agreement written on a napkin. A wedding venue circulating in the pool, St Vincent's Church in East Hampton, could not be confirmed and is not published here.
stops.campa: His son Max Samuel is born in June, and he marries the boy's mother, the actor Amy Irving, in November, in that order. The birth turns him back toward the religion he spent his adolescence hiding: he begins keeping the holidays and raising the boy inside them, and he starts saying in interviews that he has become a Jewish father. The marriage lasts four years. A prenuptial agreement the two of them wrote on a napkin is thrown out by a judge, and Irving leaves with a settlement reported at a hundred million dollars.
stops.quote: it greatly affected me... A spirit began to ignite in me, and I became a Jewish dad
stops.quote_source: Steven Spielberg, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Steven Spielberg', article note 152, on his return to Jewish observance after the birth of his son
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'Amy Irving', for the marriage dates and the vacated prenuptial agreement

stops.name: Los Angeles, eleven nominations and no director
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1985 for the film, the Directors Guild award and the eleven Academy Award nominations; the December month is the film's release and the day is defaulted. The pool records the nominations without recording the outcome of the ceremony.
stops.campa: He takes Alice Walker's novel about a Black woman in rural Georgia beaten by her father and then by her husband across forty years, and he directs it with no shark in it, no spaceship, and no truck. The industry does not know what to do with the result, and neither, for some time, do the critics. The Directors Guild of America gives him its award for best direction. The Academy gives the film eleven nominations and leaves him out of the five it nominates for directing.
suggested_refs: Alice Walker, The Color Purple (1982); Directors Guild of America award records for 1985

stops.name: Shanghai, the boy interned
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1987; month and day defaulted. Correction carried: Wikipedia's wording is the first American film shot in Shanghai since the 1940s, not the 1930s. Six Academy Award nominations, no wins.
stops.campa: He takes a crew to Shanghai, the first American production to film there since the 1940s, for a story about a British boy separated from his parents by the Japanese invasion and interned for the rest of the war. The boy survives by trading, flattering, and forgetting, and when his parents are returned to him at the end they are strangers whose faces he has to be told to recognise. Critics who had called him a maker of toys write about this one differently. Six Academy Award nominations, and no awards.
suggested_refs: J. G. Ballard, Empire of the Sun (1984), the autobiographical novel behind the film
sources: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences filmography records

stops.name: Pico Boulevard, his mother's dairy restaurant
stops.date_confidence: the restaurant is attested and the years run across the 1980s and 1990s; the date here is an ordering device only. The coordinate is derived from the Pico Boulevard address; a coordinate circulating in the pool sat about a kilometre south of Pico in Cheviot Hills, and the restaurant's own contact page returns a 404.
stops.campa: His mother, Leah Adler, keeps a small kosher dairy restaurant on Pico Boulevard: blintzes, kugel, no meat at any table, and the proprietor working the room herself and asking after everyone. She runs it for years, well into her old age, and she is not shy about whose mother she is. Strangers cross Los Angeles to eat there and to stand near it. Her son, at seven and eight and nine, was ashamed that the house kept Orthodox observance, and has said so in print, and asked God to forgive him for saying it.
stops.quote: It isn't something I enjoy admitting... but when I was seven, eight, nine years old, God forgive me, I was embarrassed because we were Orthodox Jews.
stops.quote_source: Steven Spielberg, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Steven Spielberg', article note 30
suggested_refs: The Milky Way restaurant, West Pico Boulevard, Los Angeles, operated by Leah Adler
sources: Joseph McBride, Steven Spielberg: A Biography (1997)

stops.name: Orlando, the ride that says goodbye by name
stops.date_confidence: attested: E.T. Adventure opened at Universal Studios Florida on 7 June 1990, cost roughly 40 million dollars, and the animatronic addresses guests by a name they give at the entrance. Spielberg's personal attendance at the opening is not documented in the pool.
stops.campa: At Universal Studios Florida a forty-million-dollar dark ride opens in which guests pedal bicycles over a model city, and at the end an animatronic creature says goodbye to each of them by name, having been handed the name at the queue. The film it comes from has been in the world eight years. In 1994 the Library of Congress will enter E.T. in the National Film Registry; in October 2012, for the film's thirtieth anniversary, six Madame Tussauds museums will unveil wax figures of the creature on the same day.
suggested_refs: E.T. Adventure, Universal Studios Florida, opened 7 June 1990

segments.name: Krakow, and the Archive That Followed

stops.name: Universal City, the dinosaurs made of arithmetic
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1993 for release, three Academy Awards, and passing E.T. as the highest-grossing film; month and day defaulted. Principal photography ran in 1992. The satellite supervision from Poland is well attested in production accounts but is not primary-sourced in the pool.
stops.campa: He shoots a novel about a park of resurrected dinosaurs and, partway through, decides the animals will be computed rather than built out of rods and rubber. Principal photography runs through 1992. Jurassic Park passes E.T. to become the highest-grossing film ever made and takes three Academy Awards. He finishes its effects and its sound from Poland, over satellite links, in the evenings, after days spent photographing the liquidation of a ghetto.
suggested_refs: Don Shay and Jody Duncan, The Making of Jurassic Park (1993)

stops.name: Krakow, the ghetto restaged where it stood
stops.date_confidence: attested: principal photography began 1 March 1993 in Krakow. The phrase blood money is attested inside quotation marks in the Wikipedia article on the film, footnoted to McBride (1997), p. 416, and applies to his forgone directing salary rather than to profits; the book itself could not be opened here.
stops.campa: Principal photography begins on the first of March in Podgorze, the district where the ghetto stood, in black and white, much of it handheld. He takes no salary for the film and calls what the salary would have been blood money. He restages the liquidation on the ground where the liquidation happened, in front of the buildings whose windows people were shot out of. Some of it is shot on the exact spot: the same street, the same rise where Schindler sat on his horse above the town and watched.
stops.quote: We actually shot the entire sequence on the same spot where Schindler was sitting atop his horse.
stops.quote_source: Steven Spielberg, quoted in The New Yorker, 'Steven Spielberg at Seventy' (2017)
suggested_refs: Thomas Keneally, Schindler's Ark (1982); the Podgorze ghetto wall fragments, Krakow
sources: The New Yorker, 'Steven Spielberg at Seventy' (2017)
Joseph McBride, Steven Spielberg: A Biography (1997), p. 416

stops.name: Oswiecim, the set outside the gate
stops.date_confidence: tradition and widely reported production detail, not confirmed to primary-source level here: the production was not permitted to film inside Auschwitz-Birkenau and built a set outside the gates. The date is set inside the March to May 1993 shoot; the exact day is not in the pool.
stops.campa: The production is not permitted to film inside the camp. So it builds a mirror of the gatehouse on the far side of the fence and shoots the arrival of the train from outside looking in, with the actual place standing behind the replica in every frame. In the film a women's transport is misrouted here, and the sequence that follows, a shower that turns out to deliver water, has been argued over ever since by people who think it should never have been staged at all.
suggested_refs: The Auschwitz-Birkenau Memorial and Museum, Oswiecim; the replica gatehouse built outside its perimeter in 1993
sources: widely reported production accounts of the 1993 filming restrictions

stops.name: Los Angeles, the sixty-sixth Academy Awards
stops.date_confidence: attested: the ceremony fell on 21 March 1994 and the film took seven awards including best picture and best director. The coordinate is the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion, the ceremony's venue; the pool names the city but not the hall.
stops.campa: At the sixty-sixth Academy Awards, on the twenty-first of March 1994, the film takes seven awards, best picture and best director among them, and he is called up at last, in the room that passed him over for Jaws and for The Color Purple. He has been the most commercially successful director alive for close to twenty years and has never before won this. A second award for direction follows five years later, for Saving Private Ryan. He is forty-seven.
suggested_refs: 66th Academy Awards ceremony records, 21 March 1994, Dorothy Chandler Pavilion

stops.name: University of Southern California, the fifty-two thousand testimonies
stops.date_confidence: attested: foundation 1994, some 52,000 testimonies in 56 countries by 2001, move onto the USC campus in 2006. The pool gives the year only; the month here is set to follow the March ceremony and order the segment. The Steven Spielberg Digital Yiddish Library is attested as the digitiser of Medem's memoir but is the National Yiddish Book Center's archive in Massachusetts, a namesake relation and not a place he travelled to.
stops.campa: Survivors come to the sets in Poland and afterwards to his office wanting to tell him what happened to them, and there are more of them than one man can sit with. He founds the Survivors of the Shoah Visual History Foundation and sends interviewers into fifty-six countries; by 2001 the archive holds some fifty-two thousand video testimonies, each one a person talking to a camera for as long as they need to talk. In 2006 it moves onto the campus of the university that would not admit him. The digital Yiddish library that carries his name holds, among its scans, Vladimir Medem's memoir of the Bund.
suggested_refs: USC Shoah Foundation Visual History Archive, sfi.usc.edu; the Steven Spielberg Digital Yiddish Library at the National Yiddish Book Center, which digitised Vladimir Medem's Fun mayn lebn
sources: vladimir_medem.journey.json, quote_source for Fun mayn lebn

stops.name: Universal City, DreamWorks SKG
stops.date_confidence: attested: founded 12 October 1994 with Jeffrey Katzenberg and David Geffen. Correction carried: DreamWorks SKG was at 100 Universal City Plaza, not Glendale; Glendale is DreamWorks Animation, a separate entity. The AFI Life Achievement Award is attested to 1995.
stops.campa: He founds a studio with Jeffrey Katzenberg and David Geffen: film, animation, television, music and games under one roof, the first new Hollywood studio in half a century, and it operates out of the same lot he has worked from since 1968. Under its name he makes Amistad, about the Africans who seized a schooner and argued their way to freedom in an American court. The American Film Institute gives him its Life Achievement Award the following year, the twenty-third person so honoured, at forty-eight.
suggested_refs: DreamWorks SKG, 100 Universal City Plaza; afi.com, 'AFI Life Achievement Award: Steven Spielberg' (1995)
sources: afi.com, AFI Life Achievement Award records

stops.name: Omaha Beach, the landing shot as newsreel
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1998 for release; month and day defaulted. Correction carried: the Best Director award came at the 71st Academy Awards on 21 March 1999, not in 1998. The coordinate is the represented location, Omaha Beach; the shoot took place at Curracloe, County Wexford, Ireland.
stops.campa: He opens the film with the Omaha Beach landing shot as though a newsreel cameraman had gone in with the first wave: the shutter angle wrong, water on the lens, the sound cutting out where a man's hearing goes. War films made after it copy the look. The beach is not Normandy. It is Curracloe strand in County Wexford, with Irish Army reservists standing in for the American dead, directed by a man who has been listening to his father's war stories since Arizona. The Academy gives him a second award for direction the following March.

stops.name: Los Angeles, the city of 2054
